stories.headline: Anthropic launches Claude Ship to help developers ship code faster
stories.script: Our lead story today. Anthropic said on Monday it has launched Claude Ship, a tool meant to help developers release code more quickly. According to The Economic Times, it reviews changes, fixes problems and determines which updates can be merged into the main code, following rules set by a team.

stories.headline: Honor launches 700 series with rear displays and 9,000mAh batteries
stories.script: In China. Honor on Monday unveiled its 700 smartphone series in China, TechNode reports, with every model featuring a rear display and a 9,000mAh battery. Prices start at RMB 3,399 before subsidies. The 700S, 700 and 700 Pro are open for preorder, and sales begin on November 27. The rear screen acts as a viewfinder so users can take selfies with the main cameras, and it also shows notifications, personalised images and AI interactions. Honor has included its YOYO Doubao assistant, which offers voice chat, English practice and AI-designed rear-screen artwork. An optical sensor on the back measures heart rate, blood oxygen and heart-rate variability. The handsets use MagicOS 11 and offer 80W wired charging.
stories.whyThisMatters: Honor on Monday unveiled its 700 smartphone series in China, TechNode reports, with every model featuring a rear display and a 9,000mAh battery.
keyPoints: Honor launches 700 series with rear displays and 9,000mAh batteries

stories.headline: Kate Bush and Grace Jones urge Australian government not to legalise AI ‘theft’
stories.script: In Asia. Kate Bush, Grace Jones and Sir Ian Rankin are among 7,000 artists and creative workers worldwide urging the Australian government not to weaken copyright law, the Guardian reports. Their appeal asks Labor not to allow the work of the world's creators to be legally taken on Australian soil. The campaign is the latest in a global backlash against artificial intelligence companies seeking looser copyright rules. It came on the same day a long-awaited parliamentary committee released a lengthy report recommending copyright reform in Australia. Labor MP Jo Briskey, who chairs the committee, told the paper that existing copyright laws stop frontier AI models from training on Australian content. Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the recording industry association Aria, said any attempt to dilute those protections would harm creatives.
stories.whyThisMatters: Kate Bush, Grace Jones and Sir Ian Rankin are among 7,000 artists and creative workers worldwide urging the Australian government not to weaken copyright law, the Guardian reports.

stories.headline: Google Launches Initiative to Support Indian Startups With AI, Cloud Infra
stories.script: Turning to India. Google has launched Momentum, an initiative aimed at strengthening its backing for Indian startups, Analytics India Magazine reports. The programme gives founders access to AI technologies, cloud infrastructure, engineering know-how and global platforms. It extends the work of the Google for Startups Accelerator programmes, which have run in India for a decade, and is meant to help founders build products, put AI solutions into use and move into new markets. Google has previously supported 277 Indian startups, and a large share of its alumni have continued operating. The wider strategy also includes technical mentoring and access to enterprise customers, with the goal of helping the country's startup ecosystem grow.
stories.whyThisMatters: Google has launched Momentum, an initiative aimed at strengthening its backing for Indian startups, Analytics India Magazine reports.
keyPoints: Google Launches Initiative to Support Indian Startups With AI, Cloud Infra

stories.headline: Meta launches Muse in UK the AI agent that can do your Christmas shopping
stories.script: Around the world. Meta is bringing its Muse AI assistant to the UK, pitching it as a way for shoppers to avoid the Christmas crowds, the Guardian reports. Mark Zuckerberg's company is encouraging users to give the assistant access to their apps and even let it handle purchases on the high street. In the US, Muse has proved popular, downloaded millions of times and ranked first on Google's free app store and second on Apple's. People can use it as a standalone app or inside WhatsApp, Meta's messaging service. Users are invited to personalise the assistant with a name, appearance and personality, then chat with it or hand over jobs such as writing an email, arranging travel or picking up holiday gifts. Meta said the assistant could handle everything from festive shopping to organising school schedules.
stories.whyThisMatters: Meta is bringing its Muse AI assistant to the UK, pitching it as a way for shoppers to avoid the Christmas crowds, the Guardian reports.
keyPoints: Meta launches Muse in UK the AI agent that can do your Christmas shopping

stories.headline: OpenAI and Cisco launch Shirudo, an open-source tool to shield Linux systems from exploits
stories.script: Turning to the United States. OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo, an open-source security tool that protects running Linux systems from known weaknesses without a software update or a restart, Analytics India Magazine reports. It relies on a Linux technology called eBPF to watch what a system is doing and block specific malicious behaviour. The protection comes as small programs called shields, each aimed at a vulnerable part of a piece of software, so the application can stay online. In a demonstration, a shield written with OpenAI's Codex stopped a Java4Shell exploit aimed at a live Elasticsearch service: malicious input was rejected while the service kept running. OpenAI president Greg Brockman said that finding a bug today does not mean every system can be patched tomorrow, and that the tool is meant to protect systems while teams build and roll out a permanent fix.

stories.headline: Google Search’s AI Mode can now tap into Drive and Wallet for more personalized responses
stories.script: Elsewhere. Google said on Monday it is extending Personal Intelligence, a feature within AI Mode in Search, to Google Drive, Google Wallet and the Gemini app, TechCrunch reports. Personal Intelligence aims to give users answers tailored to their circumstances by linking with their Google apps and drawing on details from their online lives. It already works with Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Photos. The expansion lets Google make greater use of the large amount of user data already held across its own services, giving it the ability to offer personalised experiences that competitors cannot match. Because some people may not want AI examining their Wallet or Drive, linking those apps is optional, and users can switch Personal Intelligence on or off whenever they choose.
stories.whyThisMatters: Google said on Monday it is extending Personal Intelligence, a feature within AI Mode in Search, to Google Drive, Google Wallet and the Gemini app, TechCrunch reports.

stories.headline: ByteDance opens invitation-only beta for Xiaodou personal AI assistant
stories.script: In China. ByteDance's Doubao team has opened a beta of Xiaodou, a personal AI assistant, TechNode reports. Access on Tuesday was by invitation code only, and testers receive a set of free usage credits. Xiaodou is a separate product from the main Doubao app, and it is pitched as an assistant that can take the initiative to help users finish tasks rather than only answer questions. ByteDance says Xiaodou's features will gradually be brought into the main Doubao app, so the beta gives the company a place to try out personal-agent features before releasing them to Doubao's much larger audience. The announcement gave no timetable for opening Xiaodou to everyone or for moving individual features into Doubao.
stories.whyThisMatters: ByteDance's Doubao team has opened a beta of Xiaodou, a personal AI assistant, TechNode reports.
keyPoints: ByteDance opens invitation-only beta for Xiaodou personal AI assistant
TechNode

stories.headline: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
stories.script: From the research desk. The researchers behind a paper titled Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control are tackling how to generate long, controllable movement in real time, something animated characters and humanoid robots need when instructions and destinations change mid-motion. Current diffusion methods that build movement step by step struggle to recall events from far back, and their repeated noise-removal passes slow them down. The team's system, built on the Mamba architecture, combines short-range attention, recurrent states that can be resumed, and a feature called persistent content memory, which turns compressed motion history and text cues into continually updated slots the model can draw on.
